sections.title: Identification
sections.text: Suillus grevillei is a bolete with a convex cap that flattens with age, usually 3–15 cm across. Its smooth, shiny cuticle is sticky or slimy in wet weather and ranges from lemon or golden yellow to orange and golden brown; the skin separates readily from the flesh.

sections.title: Pores, stem and flesh
sections.text: The fertile surface consists of tubes ending in small angular pores, lemon to golden yellow, which may turn brown when damaged. The tubes are adnate to slightly decurrent. The solid stem is usually 4.5–10 cm long and usually bears a conspicuous upper ring, pale to yellowish brown, though the ring may be absent; the stem is yellow above and often more golden or brown below. The flesh is pale to lemon yellow, rather soft, and generally changes little on exposure to air; smell and taste are mild. The spore print is yellowish brown to cinnamon brown.

sections.title: Habitat and similar species
sections.text: This ectomycorrhizal fungus grows on the ground with larches (Larix), often in groups, from late summer into autumn. The sticky yellow-orange cap, yellow pores and ring help separate it from many boletes, but identification should consider the host tree and all features together. Suillus luteus also has a ring, but associates with pines and often has glandular dots on its stem.

sections.title: Edibility and caution
sections.text: The DGfM and VAPKO list this species as edible. Such lists do not establish the identity of a specimen: never eat a wild mushroom based on an image alone.

traits: Cap usually 3–15 cm across, convex then flattening, smooth, shiny and sticky in wet weather, yellow to orange or golden brown
Small angular lemon-yellow to golden pores, sometimes browning when bruised; tubes adnate to slightly decurrent
Solid stem usually 4.5–10 cm long, yellow above an upper ring that is usually present but may be absent, more golden or brown below
Pale to lemon-yellow, rather soft flesh, generally little changed by exposure to air; mild smell and taste
On the ground in ectomycorrhizal association with larches (Larix), from late summer into autumn
safetyNote: The DGfM and VAPKO list Suillus grevillei as edible. An edibility list cannot identify a specimen: never eat a wild mushroom based on a photo alone. If symptoms follow ingestion, contact poison control or emergency services immediately.
